answer.answer:
Regulatory exposure in this record attaches less to the robots themselves than to what surrounds them: collaborative work alongside people, bespoke digital fabrication technology, concrete printing and on-site printing each have to clear a compliance requirement before they can proceed, whereas robotic assembly, robotic drilling, the robotic arm and unmanned mobile vehicles carry no dependency of their own on regulatory or legal concern. The four requirements are not equal in weight: the compliance requirement on bespoke technology is carried by 9 of the 50 coded cases, against 2 each for human-robot interaction, additive manufacturing and on-site digital fabrication. Two of the four are sharpest in practice: certifying printed concrete walls for structural strength, fire safety and durability, and getting on-site printing through an alternative-means approval route. In the deployed Japanese records, regulation appears as a stated reason for adopting the process rather than as a reported obstacle, so treat it as a design constraint to be engineered for, not a barrier the record shows anyone failing at.

**Where the regulatory requirement sits**

Four dependency edges in the graph terminate in RI18 "Regulatory/legal concern" (Risk), all of them backed by standards-grade evidence, and in each the compliance requirement is upstream of the activity:

- AT3 "Bespoke DFAB technology" dependsOn RI18, carried by 9 of the 50 coded cases [1]: robot technology design and integration depends on baseline safety-standard compliance [1]. This is the widest-carried of the four by a factor of four or five.
- CO6 "Human-robot interaction" dependsOn RI18, carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases [1]: human-robot collaborative work depends on compliance with robot safety standards [1].
- PR3 "Additive manufacturing" dependsOn RI18, carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases [1]: 3D printed concrete walls require certification against acceptance criteria for structural strength, fire safety and durability [1].
- PR8 "On-site DFAB" dependsOn RI18, carried by 2 of the 50 coded cases [1]: on-site 3D concrete printing deployment proceeds via an alternative-means approval pathway [1].

RI18 itself is drawn on by 12 of the 50 coded cases [1]. These four are the complete set of standards-graded edges reaching it, but the context does not list every edge touching RI18 at other evidence grades, so this is not the whole of the regulatory picture.

On the enablers the question was read into: PR4 "Robotic assembly" carries 4 inbound and 6 outbound edges, all listed, and is drawn on by 13 of the 50 coded cases [1], and none of them reaches RI18; RE2 "Robotic arm" carries 1 inbound and 1 outbound edge and is drawn on by 22 cases [1], again neither touching RI18; PR19 "Robotic drilling", drawn on by 9 cases, carries no dependency edges at all [1], as does RE15 "Unmanned mobile vehicle", drawn on by 25 cases [1]. The regulatory load is therefore carried by the process and technology context, not by the machine class.

**The safety side, which is adjacent but distinct**

RI20 "Work safety concern" carries 3 inbound edges, all listed, and is drawn on by 13 of the 50 coded cases [1]. Three mitigations run into it, and they differ in reach: AT10 "Human assistance" mitigates RI20 in 8 of the 50 cases, via a passive exoskeleton that reduced lumbar erector spinae activity by 11 to 33 per cent MVC [1]; CO2 "3D scanning/RFID/sensing" mitigates RI20 in 7 cases through speed-and-separation monitoring that maintains a minimum protective distance [1]; and CO6 "Human-robot interaction" mitigates RI20 in 4 cases through power-and-force-limiting operation within biomechanical limits [1]. The last two are standards-grade. So the same standards that impose the compliance requirement also supply the two technical routes out of the contact-injury risk.

**What the deployed records show**

The census records here name regulation as an adoption driver rather than a failure mode. census_RXH5-1 performs assembly, steelwork and welding on the structural core, adopted to address regulation, at technology readiness level 9 [2], manufactured by Firm_027 and working in steel [3]. The clearest match to the printing-certification path is census_RXM4-3, adopted to address regulation, performing 3d printing, assembly and concrete work on the structural core, at technology readiness level 7 [4]; it is manufactured by Firm_115, uses concrete, and is the census record of RP15 [3], which is deployed as a mobile robot and off-site, at technology readiness level 7 [5]. That pairing is the one deployed case in front of me that sits on both the additive-manufacturing and on-site printing requirements, and it is the lowest-maturity of the structural-core group.

Others show regulation combined with further drivers: census_RXT4-1 was adopted to address integration, market and regulation, performing assembly, material handling and timber joinery cutting at technology readiness level 9 [6], developed by Firm_174 in timber [3]; census_RXH12-1 for quality, integration and regulation, assembly and timber joinery cutting, at technology readiness level 9 [7]; census_RXM29-4 for integration and regulation, material handling, at technology readiness level 5 [8]; and census_RXM1-1 for regulation, performing inspection, at technology readiness level 7 [9]. census_RXH9-1b, adopted to address cost, integration and regulation on the structural core at technology readiness level 9 [10], is manufactured by Firm_160 and is the census record of RP5 [3].

The context does not record which enablers these individual cases draw on, so I cannot say that any one of them exhibits RI18 or the specific compliance edges above; the 12-case figure for RI18 comes from the coded record as a whole.
